title: I Tested the Dell XPS 13 and MacBook Neo Side by Side. The Results Surprised Me
author: Luke Larsen
text: All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.Ever since the MacBook Neo was announced this spring, I've been looking for a serious alternative. Not a cheap knockoff that sacrifices quality for price. No, no. I was hunting for a Windows laptop with the same goal as the MacBook Neo—hiding its compromises and delivering an otherwise premium laptop at a lower cost. For months, it was crickets.Then, the Dell XPS 13 showed up on my doorstep, and it understood the assignment. For many reasons, this was the one I'd been waiting for. But the question remains: Is it actually the better budget laptop? The answer surprised me when I dug into the testing.Hidden CompromisesWhen the MacBook Neo was originally announced, it was a shocker. Apple coming in at the $599 price point for the base configuration felt unreal. Apple had never in its history brought the MacBook to such a low price. Even at its new $699 starting price, it's in unprecedented territory. Importantly, this encroached on the territory of Windows laptops, where it has traditionally had a monopoly.Photograph: Luke LarsenAnd while many Windows laptops are available at this price, they suffer from many of the same problems, such as cheap materials or corners cut with low-quality displays and touchpads. Even a cheap laptop I like quite a bit, like the HP OmniBook 5 (with the Snapdragon X Plus), has a weak point in its touchpad.AppleMacBook Neo$699 Amazon$699 Walmart$699 AppleBut the Dell XPS 13 sought to match the MacBook Neo's premium quality in nearly every aspect. It has the same starting price of $699 (or $599 for students). It's exactly the same size at just a half-inch thick, so when the lid is closed and you're holding it, it feels just as portable. The XPS 13 weighs 2.2 pounds, half a pound lighter than the MacBook Neo. The Neo isn't heavy, but holding both in your hands, the difference is noticeable. That's the first point in favor of the XPS 13.Despite a slightly smaller screen (13 inches, measured diagonally), the MacBook Neo sits taller than the XPS 13 when the lid is open. That's because the XPS 13's 13.4-inch display is surrounded by much smaller bezels—particularly the bottom, which gives the XPS 13 a more modern look. The white keyboard and flashier color options of the MacBook Neo certainly have their appeal, especially since the XPS 13 comes in only two shades of silver. But in general, more screen real estate and smaller dimensions are preferable, especially if you want to travel on an airplane with your laptop.And then there's the screen itself. Most $700 laptops have mediocre screens that aren't bright enough and have poor colors. I never expected Apple to skimp on the display, of course, and it didn't. It goes up to 509 nits (as tested) and has decent color reproduction. But the XPS 13 is better in three ways. First, it has a touchscreen, which MacBooks don't (yet) have. That's a nice addition for an entry-level model. It also has a 120-Hz refresh rate, which gives the screen fast, fluid responsiveness that not even the MacBook Air has. Again, that's a feature that's exceedingly rare to find on a budget-level laptop. Lastly, the XPS 13 has better color saturation, specifically on the Adobe RGB and P3 color scales. It's actually one of the better IPS screens I've tested on a laptop, and it's as sharp as the MacBook Neo.None of these are weak points of the MacBook Neo, but it's worth noting that the XPS 13 has it beat in a number of these areas. That's also true of the keyboard and trackpad. Both are excellent on these laptops, and I found myself comfortable using them right off the bat. Again, trackpads in particular can be a sore spot for budget Windows laptops, but Dell smartly didn't skimp on it. Apple's the one that compromised on the keyboard, both by not including Touch ID in the base model and by removing backlighting (which the XPS 13 includes).Ports, Storage, and VideoconferencingI already mentioned the display and the portability, but there are a few other places where the XPS 13 is the clear winner. The first is the USB-C ports. Both devices have two, but the XPS 13 splits them, so one is on the left side, and one is on the right side. I really like this decision, as it allows you to charge the device from either side. Then, there's the speed of these USB-C ports. One of the USB-C ports on the MacBook Neo is an outdated USB 2 port. Not only is it slow for file transfers, but it also can't natively output to an external display. Both USB-C ports on the XPS 13 are USB 3.2 Gen 2, which can each support a 4K display and transfer data at up to 10 Gbps.DellXPS 13 (2026)$700 Dell (8 GB)$900 Dell (16 GB)The Neo does have an advantage when it comes to ports, though. It has a headphone jack, whereas the XPS 13 doesn't. This might be less of a big deal today than it was in the past, but I prefer laptops to keep them.The XPS 13 comes with 512 GB of storage in both the base and upgraded models. The MacBook Neo base model comes only with 256 GB, and you'll need to upgrade to the Touch ID model for 521 GB. On top of that, Dell's laptop uses faster storage. That's a winning combination.Most PopularBuying GuidesGive Your Back a Break With Our Favorite Office ChairsBy Julian ChokkattuGearWe Bought a $500 Counterfeit Rolex So Good, Even Rolex Didn’t Spot ItBy Alistair CharltonGearThere’s a Very Simple Reason Why You Love the Slate TruckBy Jeremy WhitePhonesYou Can Finally Buy a Fairphone in the USBy Julian ChokkattuThe videoconferencing setup is similarly good. Both webcams are 1080p. Though the image processing is a bit better on the MacBook Neo, the XPS 13 includes an IR camera for logging in without a password. The base configuration of the Neo doesn't have Touch ID, so you have to type a password to log in, change settings, and pay online.The RAM ProblemApple never claimed the MacBook Neo was a powerhouse. Built on an iPhone chip (the A18 Pro) and limited to 8 GB of RAM, it is clearly designed for college students and anyone with lower-level computing needs. When I tested it initially, I found that if I wasn't paying attention, it was easy to let open applications, tons of browser tabs, and background tasks slow the computer down, with the main bottleneck being the 8 GB of RAM. Apple hasn't sold a MacBook with 8 GB of RAM since 2024, but the company has always insisted that its unified memory system means it doesn't need as much capacity as a Windows PC. But is that really true? Now that we have a very comparable Windows system with 8 GB of RAM as well, it'll be easy to test just how true Apple's claims are.Photograph: Luke LarsenThe bad news is that both devices took very little effort to use up the available memory. Playing a YouTube video with various news sites open in six Google Chrome tabs was enough to use over 90 percent of the 8 GB. Neither Windows nor macOS feels optimized for a computer with just 8 GB of RAM these days, no doubt from all the AI-infused tasks running in the background. Now, just because you're getting dangerously close to reaching 100 percent of the memory utilization, that doesn't mean your computer instantly freezes up. It takes a lot to get these systems to grind to a halt, but with a 16-GB laptop, you'll spend much less time managing what tabs and applications you have open. On the other hand, if you're a student coming from a cheap Chromebook or hand-me-down computer, these laptops will feel like a nice upgrade.Most PopularBuying GuidesGive Your Back a Break With Our Favorite Office ChairsBy Julian ChokkattuGearWe Bought a $500 Counterfeit Rolex So Good, Even Rolex Didn’t Spot ItBy Alistair CharltonGearThere’s a Very Simple Reason Why You Love the Slate TruckBy Jeremy WhitePhonesYou Can Finally Buy a Fairphone in the USBy Julian ChokkattuThe XPS 13 has a fan inside, while the MacBook Neo is passively cooled. Under a heavy load you can hear that fan spin up in the XPS 13, whereas the Neo is completely silent. Both laptops get excellent battery life—enough to get through a full day of class or work. That's another area where laptops at this price tended to suffer in the past.But the big difference between these two laptops is how you can configure them. Both start at $700 ($699 for the Neo, to be exact), and you get one upgrade option. For an extra $100, you can move up to the MacBook Neo with 512 GB of storage and Touch ID built in. On the other hand, the Dell XPS 13 has a $900 model that's identical to the base model, except it has 16 GB of RAM. So yes, the 16-GB version of the XPS 13 is $100 more expensive. But it's better in nearly every way, and it's likely the best laptop you can buy for less than $1,000.And even when comparing the 8-GB model, the XPS 13 handily beats the MacBook Neo in tons of small ways. It has a better display, a backlit keyboard, two USB ports—one on each side—that support charging and 4K monitors, and it's more portable. It does all that while looking super sharp and feeling just as premium as the Neo. While I think everyone should buy a 16-GB laptop, at the 8-GB level, the Dell XPS 13 is the better laptop no matter how you slice it.
